scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Montea, widely termed moutya, originated in the Seychelles at the beginning of the eighteenth century following the arrival of French colonists and enslaved Africans.
Practiced far from plantation grounds, the dance was carried out at night deep in the forest as psychological comfort against the conditions of slavery.
Through rhythmic gatherings around open fires, enslaved people preserved communal solidarity and voiced social commentary.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a nocturnal refuge from slavery, moutya serves as an homage to ancestors and an expression of the aspiration to freedom.
Long shunned as transgressive or risqué prior to the late 1970s, it was embraced post-independence as a core vessel of Seychellois Creole identity and inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance takes place around an open fire, starting at a moderate tempo and progressively accelerating.
Dancers maintain an upright upper torso while executing foot stamps and rolling their hips.
Female dancers rhythmically move their skirts.
Watch for Roulant des hanches, Frappant du pied, Mouvement de jupes.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is driven by a single goatskin drum, or narrow frame drums made of dried goat hide, which drummers lightly heat over the bonfire before playing and repeatedly throughout the evening to retain tension.
Traditional accompaniment also incorporates everyday utilitarian instruments such as cooking pots, utensils, and coconuts.
Listen for the Goatskin frame drum, Cooking pots, Kitchen utensils, Coconuts.

A single resonant goatskin drum, periodically tightened over flames, lays down an accelerating pulse. Call-and-response vocals cut through the night, supported by the clatter of kitchen pots, utensils, and coconut shells around a crackling fire.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The setting is outdoors centered around a bonfire, historically set in forests at night away from plantations.
Female dancers wear long skirts which are actively manipulated and moved during the choreography.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Secretary General for Culture David André championed the successful 2021 UNESCO intangible cultural heritage inscription.
Penda Choppy, director of the Creole Institute, characterized the dance as an ancestral tribute and aspiration for unobtained freedom.
In contemporary Seychelles, traditional practice is distinguished from 'moutya otentik,' which is staged for tourists.
Moutya was introduced by enslaved Africans in the early 18th century, undergoing creolization in the Seychelles.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Montea is sibling of Sega: Similar Indian Ocean traditional dance, though moutya exhibits more pronounced suggestive movements.
Montea is sibling of Séga mauricien: Mauritian folk genre sharing historic slave roots and creolization dynamics with moutya.
Montea is sibling of Maloya: Réunionese Afro-diasporic tradition sharing percussive bonfire heritage and emotional resonance.
